question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 7 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad V = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices $A,$ $\Sigma,$ and $V$ shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the second column of $U?$
question.explanation:
Recall that if $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ and $\sigma_i \neq 0,$ then the $i$th column of $U$ can be found as

\[ \mathbf{u}_i = \dfrac{1}{\sigma_i} A\mathbf{v}_i, \]

where $\mathbf v_i$ is the $i$th column of the matrix $V.$

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that the singular values are $\sigma_1=9$ and $\sigma_2=1.$ Therefore, the second column of $U$ is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_2 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_2} A\mathbf{v}_2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{1} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 7 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} . \end{align*}

example.title: Determining the Columns of the First Matrix Given Part of a Singular Value Decomposition

question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} -5 & 4 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad V = \begin{bmatrix} v_{11} & v_{12} \\ v_{21} & v_{22} \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the value of $|v_{11}| + |v_{21}|?$
question.explanation:
If $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ the columns of $V$ must be the right singular vectors of $A,$ i.e., the unit eigenvectors of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that the singular values are $\sigma_1=7$ and $\sigma_2=3.$ So, the first column of $V$ corresponds to the singular value $\sigma_1=7.$

Hence, we need to find a unit eigenvector of $A^T \!A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_1 = \sigma_1^2=49.$

  • Computing $A^T \! A,$ we obtain \begin{align*} A^T \! A &= \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 4 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^T \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 4 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 4 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 4 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 41 & -16 \\ -16 & 17 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

  • Computing $A^T \! A - 49 I,$ we get \[ A^T \! A - 49 I = \begin{bmatrix} 41 & -16 \\ -16 & 17 \end{bmatrix} - 49 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -8 & -16 \\ -16 & -32 \end{bmatrix} \]

  • Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T\!A-49I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm, we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v} }{\| \mathbf{v} \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore,

\[ |v_{11}| + |v_{21}| = \left| -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \right| + \left| \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \right| = \dfrac3{\sqrt{5}}. \]

example.title: Finding the Columns of the Third Matrix Given Part of a Singular Value Decomposition

question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 6 \\ -9 & 4 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix}, \quad V = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{17}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} & \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices $A,$ $\Sigma,$ and $V$ shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the first column of $U?$
question.explanation:
Recall that if $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ and $\sigma_i \neq 0,$ then the $i$th column of $U$ can be found as

\[ \mathbf{u}_i = \dfrac{1}{\sigma_i} A\mathbf{v}_i, \]

where $\mathbf v_i$ is the $i$th column of the matrix $V.$

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that the singular values are $\sigma_1=10$ and $\sigma_2=7.$ Therefore, the first column of $U$ is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_1 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_1} A\mathbf{v}_1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{10} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 6 \\ -9 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{10} \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \dfrac{40}{\sqrt{17}} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} 8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices $A$ and $\Sigma$ shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$
question.explanation:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

  • Step 1. Compute $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} A^T \! A &= \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}^T \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 3 \\ -3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 73 & -24 \\ -24 & 9 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

  • Step 2. Find the singular values: From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that $\sigma_1=9$ and $\sigma_2=1.$

  • Step 3. Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T \! A$):

    • For $\lambda_1=\sigma_1^2=81,$ we have \begin{align*} A^T \! A - 81 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 73 & -24 \\ -24 & 9 \end{bmatrix} - 81 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -8 & -24 \\ -24 & -72 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 81I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives a unit eigenvector
      \[ \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

    • For $\lambda_2=\sigma_2^2=1,$ we have \begin{align*} A^T \! A - I &= \begin{bmatrix} 73 & -24 \\ -24 & 9 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 72 & -24 \\ -24 & 8 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives a unit eigenvector
      \[ \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • Step 4. Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

    • First, we compute $\mathbf u_1\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_1 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_1} A\mathbf{v}_1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{9} \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{9} \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{27}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\dfrac{9}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix} \\[10pt] \end{align*}

    • Then, we compute $\mathbf u_2\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_2 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_2} A\mathbf{v}_2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{1} \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -3 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix} \\[10pt] \end{align*}

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V\mathbin{:}$

\[ U = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad V = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix} \]

example.title: The Singular Value Decomposition of a 2x2 Matrix

question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices $A$ and $\Sigma$ shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$
question.explanation:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

  • Step 1. Compute $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} A^T \! A &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}^T \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 8 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

  • Step 2. Find the singular values: From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that $\sigma_1=3$ and $\sigma_2=2.$

  • Step 3. Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T \! A$):

    • For $\lambda_1=\sigma_1^2=9,$ we have \begin{align*} A^T \! A - 9 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 8 \end{bmatrix} - 9 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -4& 2\\ 2& -1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 9I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives a unit eigenvector
      \[ \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

    • For $\lambda_2=\sigma_2^2=4,$ we have \begin{align*} A^T \! A - 4 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 8 \end{bmatrix} - 4 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 4I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives a unit eigenvector
      \[ \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • Step 4. Find the left singular vectors of $A.$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

    • First, we compute $\mathbf u_1\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_1 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_1} A\mathbf{v}_1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{6}{\sqrt 5} \\ -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt 5} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \\[10pt] \end{align*}

    • Then, we compute $\mathbf u_2\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_2 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_2} A\mathbf{v}_2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt 5} \\ -\dfrac{4}{\sqrt 5} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \\[10pt] \end{align*}

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V\mathbin{:}$

\[ U = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad V = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \]
